lessons.title: Sort It Out
objectives: Sort objects into groups by one feature
Explain the sorting rule using "because"
explanation: Sorting means putting things that are the same in some way into groups. We can sort by colour (all the red things together), by shape (all the circles) or by size (big and small).
The reason we put things together is the sorting rule. "These go together because they are all blue."
The same things can be sorted in different ways! Buttons could be sorted by colour, by size or by how many holes they have.

Sorting socks into pairs.

lessons.title: Which One Doesn't Belong?
objectives: Find the odd one out in a group

explanation: In an odd-one-out puzzle, all the things are alike except one. We look carefully to see what most of them share.
For example: cat, dog, cow, car. The car is the odd one out because it is not an animal.
Sometimes there is more than one good answer! In a red apple, a red car and a green apple, the car is odd (not a fruit) — or the green apple is odd (not red). What matters is a good reason.

Ivaan thought hard. "The carrot, because it's a vegetable!" "Or the banana," said Aaji, "because it's the only one you peel like that." They both were right.

lessons.title: Find the Pattern
objectives: Continue repeating and growing patterns
Explain the pattern rule
explanation: A pattern is something that repeats or changes in a regular way. Red, blue, red, blue... comes next? Red!
Some patterns grow: 1 star, 2 stars, 3 stars... The rule is "add one more each time".
To find what comes next, look for the rule. Then use the rule to predict. Logic helps us notice rules and use them.

lessons.title: If It Rains, the Ground Gets Wet
objectives: Use if-then rules to reach conclusions
Use clues to solve simple logic puzzles
explanation: An if-then rule tells us what follows from something. "If it rains, then the ground gets wet." If we know it is raining, we can conclude the ground is wet.
Careful! If the ground is wet, it might not be because of rain — maybe someone watered the plants. Good thinkers check other possibilities.
Logic puzzles give clues. "The cat is not on the bed. The cat is on the chair or the bed." So the cat must be on the chair!

vocabulary.meaning: a rule saying one thing follows from another
a piece of information that helps solve a puzzle

examples: If you drop a glass, then it may break.
If it is Sunday, then there is no school.

Ivaan checked: the plate was too high for Kiko... unless he climbed the chair. The chair had paw prints! "Mystery solved," said Ivaan.

lessons.title: Circles That Overlap
objectives: Sort items into a two-circle Venn diagram
Explain the meaning of the overlap and the outside
explanation: A Venn diagram uses overlapping circles to sort things by two rules at once. It is named after John Venn, an English logician, who popularised it in 1880.

If one circle is "animals that can fly" and the other "animals that lay eggs", the overlap holds animals that do both (like a pigeon). A bat goes only in "can fly"; a crocodile goes only in "lays eggs".
Things that fit neither rule — like a dog — go outside both circles.

vocabulary.meaning: a group with a shared feature

examples: A penguin: lays eggs but cannot fly.
A bat: flies but does not lay eggs.

story.title: The Fruit Venn
story.text: Zuri drew two hoops on the floor: "red" and "round". An apple went in the overlap — red AND round! A strawberry went only in red. An orange went only in round. A banana went outside — neither red nor round. "The overlap is for things that are both," she explained to her little brother.

lessons.title: And, Or, Not
objectives: Use and, or and not precisely
Decide whether combined statements are true or false
explanation: In logic, "and" means both parts must be true. "It is sunny AND warm" is true only if it is both sunny and warm.

"Or" means at least one part is true. "I will have tea OR juice" — in logic, having both still makes it true (this is called inclusive or). "Not" flips truth: if "it is raining" is false, "it is NOT raining" is true.
Computers use and, or and not (called Boolean operators) to search and make decisions. Searching "tigers AND India" finds pages about both.

vocabulary.meaning: at least one must be true
a sentence that is true or false

examples: "A square has 4 sides AND 4 corners" — true.
"A cat is NOT a fish" — true.

story.title: The Club Rules
story.text: Kiko's club had a rule: "To join, you must be 8 AND like puzzles." Zuri was 8 and loved puzzles — she joined! Raj was 8 but hated puzzles — not allowed. Then the rule changed to "8 OR likes puzzles." Now Raj could join, and so could Zuri's little brother, who was 6 but loved puzzles.

lessons.title: Certain or Likely?
objectives: Distinguish deductive from inductive reasoning
Explain why inductive conclusions can be overturned
explanation: Deductive reasoning moves from general rules to a certain conclusion: "All mammals breathe air. Whales are mammals. So whales breathe air." If the premises are true and the reasoning valid, the conclusion must be true.

Inductive reasoning moves from observations to a general, probable conclusion: "Every swan I have seen is white, so all swans are white." It is useful but can be wrong — Europeans believed this until black swans were recorded in Australia in 1697.
Science relies heavily on induction (observing patterns) and tests ideas deductively (predicting what should happen if an idea is true).

vocabulary.meaning: reasoning from general rules to a certain conclusion
reasoning from observations to a likely conclusion
a statement an argument starts from

examples: A detective deducing from clues.
Predicting the sun will rise tomorrow from past experience.

story.title: The Black Swan
story.text: For centuries, Europeans used "black swan" to mean something impossible — every swan anyone had seen was white. Then, in 1697, Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh's expedition saw black swans in Western Australia. One observation overturned a "certain" rule. Thinkers still use the black swan to warn that induction can fail.

lessons.title: All, Some and None
objectives: Evaluate syllogisms as valid or invalid
Explain the difference between a valid and a true argument
explanation: A syllogism is an argument with two premises and a conclusion, studied by Aristotle over 2,300 years ago. "All dogs are animals. All animals need food. So all dogs need food." This is valid.

Validity is about form: if the premises were true, would the conclusion have to be true? "All cats can fly. Tom is a cat. So Tom can fly" is valid in form — but its first premise is false, so the conclusion isn't established.
Invalid example: "All roses are flowers. Some flowers fade quickly. So some roses fade quickly." The fading flowers might not be roses! Venn diagrams help check validity.

vocabulary.meaning: an argument with two premises and a conclusion
the conclusion follows from the premises

examples: A valid but unsound syllogism about flying cats.
A Venn diagram showing roses inside flowers.

story.title: The Tricky Shopkeeper
story.text: A shopkeeper said, "All good phones are expensive. This phone is expensive. So it must be good!" Meera drew a Venn diagram: good phones inside expensive things — but expensive things could include bad phones too. "That doesn't follow," she said politely. The shopkeeper laughed and offered a discount.

lessons.title: Spot the Fallacy
objectives: Identify common logical fallacies
Respond to fallacious arguments constructively
explanation: A fallacy is an error in reasoning that makes an argument seem stronger than it is. Ad hominem attacks the person instead of the argument ("You're too young to know"). Straw man misrepresents an opponent's view to make it easier to attack.

A false dilemma presents only two options when more exist ("Either you agree with me or you hate the country"). Slippery slope claims one step will inevitably lead to extreme consequences without evidence.

Appeal to popularity says something is true because many believe it; appeal to authority relies on someone's status rather than evidence, especially outside their expertise. Post hoc assumes that because B followed A, A caused B.

vocabulary.meaning: attacking the person, not the argument
presenting only two options when more exist

examples: "Everyone's buying it, so it must be good" (appeal to popularity).
"I wore my lucky socks and we won" (post hoc).

story.title: The Debate Club
story.text: In a debate about school uniforms, Raj said, "Zuri only wants to ban uniforms because she's lazy!" The judge stopped him. "That's ad hominem — address her arguments, not her." Raj then said, "So she wants students to wear anything, even pyjamas?" "Straw man," said the judge. Raj sighed and finally answered her real point.

lessons.title: Truth Tables and Implication
objectives: Construct truth tables for AND, OR, NOT and IF-THEN
Distinguish a conditional from its converse and contrapositive
explanation: Propositional logic uses letters for statements (P, Q) and connectives: ∧ (and), ∨ (or), ¬ (not) and → (if-then). A truth table lists every combination of truth values. With two propositions, there are 4 rows.
P → Q ("if P then Q") is false only when P is true and Q is false. For example, "If it rains, the match is cancelled" is broken only if it rains and the match goes ahead.

The converse (Q → P) does not follow from P → Q. But the contrapositive (¬Q → ¬P) is logically equivalent: "If the match was not cancelled, it did not rain." George Boole's algebra of logic (1854) underlies digital circuits.

vocabulary.meaning: a statement that is true or false
a word or symbol joining propositions
negating and reversing an if-then statement

examples: A truth table for P ∧ Q with four rows.
Logic gates in a computer chip.

story.title: The Card Puzzle
story.text: Peter Wason's famous 1966 selection task shows four cards: A, K, 4, 7. Rule: "If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other." Which cards must you turn to test it? Most people pick A and 4. The answer is A and 7 — because the 7 could hide a vowel, breaking the rule. Formal logic beats intuition here.

lessons.title: Where There Is Smoke, There Is Fire
objectives: Describe the pramanas of Nyaya philosophy
Analyse the five-member Nyaya syllogism
explanation: Nyaya is one of the classical schools of Indian philosophy, systematised in the Nyaya Sutras traditionally attributed to Gautama (Akshapada), commonly dated to roughly the 2nd century CE. It studies pramanas — valid means of knowledge: perception (pratyaksha), inference (anumana), comparison (upamana) and testimony (shabda).

The Nyaya inference has five members: (1) The hill has fire (thesis). (2) Because it has smoke (reason). (3) Wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen (rule with example). (4) This hill has smoke associated with fire (application). (5) Therefore the hill has fire (conclusion). Unlike Aristotle's form, it explicitly includes an example.

Later, Navya-Nyaya ("new logic"), associated with Gangesha (around the 14th century), developed a highly precise technical language. Indian traditions also analysed debate and fallacies (hetvabhasa — "reasons that only appear valid").

vocabulary.meaning: the universal relation between reason and conclusion

examples: Inferring fire from smoke on a distant hill.
Debates in ancient Indian universities like Nalanda.

story.title: The Smoke on the Hill
story.text: A traveller saw smoke rising from a distant hill. "There must be fire," she said. Her companion asked, "How do you know? You can't see it." She replied, "Wherever I have seen smoke, I have seen fire — in kitchens, in fields. And this smoke is rising from the hill." Nyaya philosophers used this simple scene to build a whole theory of inference.

lessons.title: Updating Beliefs With Evidence
objectives: Apply base rates and Bayes' theorem informally
Distinguish correlation from causation
explanation: Real reasoning is often uncertain. Bayes' theorem, named after Thomas Bayes (published 1763), shows how to update the probability of a hypothesis when new evidence arrives.

Base rates matter. Suppose a disease affects 1 in 1,000 people and a test is 99% accurate. If you test positive, the chance you have the disease is only about 9%: among 100,000 people, about 99 of the 100 sick people test positive, but so do about 999 healthy people (1% false positives). Ignoring this is the base rate fallacy.

Correlation is not causation: ice-cream sales and drowning both rise in summer, but one doesn't cause the other — hot weather affects both (a confounding variable). Randomised controlled trials help establish causation.

vocabulary.meaning: how common something is in a population
a formula for updating probabilities with evidence
a hidden factor affecting both variables

examples: A positive result for a rare disease is often a false positive.

story.title: The Rare Disease Test
story.text: A doctor told a worried patient, "Your test was positive, but don't panic yet." She drew 1,000 dots: one red (sick), 999 blue. "The test catches the red one, but also wrongly flags about 10 blue ones. So of 11 positives, only 1 is truly sick." The patient's follow-up test came back negative. Thinking in base rates had saved a lot of fear.
